# Strings, raw strings, and characters

Almost every program touches text. In Nim, `string` is a sequence of bytes that may be changed in
place — unlike languages that treat a string as a frozen value. That difference shows up in
indexing, concatenation, and occasionally in an unexpected error message.

This chapter starts with writing text literally, then moves on to taking part of it and changing it
safely.

::: {.callout-note}
## What you will be able to do

After this chapter you can write escape sequences and raw strings, take a character or a slice of
text with indexing and slicing, tell `&` apart from `add`, and explain why `s[0] = 'N'` is
rejected when `s` is declared with `let`.
:::

## Escape sequences

Save this as `escapes.nim`, then run `nim r escapes.nim`.

```{.nim}
echo "line 1\nline 2"
echo "quote: \"ok\""
echo "backslash: \\"
echo "brace: { }"
```

```{.txt}
line 1
line 2
quote: "ok"
backslash: \
brace: { }
```

A backslash inside a string opens an *escape sequence*. `\n` becomes a new line, `\"` becomes a
quote that does not end the string, and `\\` becomes a single backslash. Note the last line: a
brace `{` is nothing special in an ordinary string. It only has meaning inside the *interpolation*
`&"..."` covered in the next chapter.

## Raw strings

Sometimes we want the backslash left exactly as it is, for example in a Windows path or a regular
expression. The `r` prefix turns off every escape:

```{.nim}
let path = r"C:\Users\nim\bin"
let pattern = r"\d+\.\d+"

echo path
echo pattern
```

```{.txt}
C:\Users\nim\bin
\d+\.\d+
```

Without `r`, `\U` and `\d` are not recognized escapes and can raise a warning. A raw string also
does not treat `"` specially, so the text above reads exactly as written.

## Multi-line strings

For text that spans several lines, use three quotes:

```{.nim}
let banner = """
line one
line two
"""

echo banner.len
echo banner
echo "END"
```

```{.txt}
18
line one
line two

END
```

Notice `len` is 18. The content is `line one\nline two\n`: 8 + 1 + 8 + 1 characters. The newline
after the opening `"""` counts, and that is a common source of counting mistakes for newcomers.
A triple-quoted raw string does not process escapes either.

## Length and indexing

`len` gives the number of bytes, and indexing starts at zero. Calling `len` is cheap: a string
keeps its length alongside its data instead of recounting every time.

```{.nim}
let s = "Nim rocks"

echo s.len
echo s[0]
echo s[^1]
echo s[0..2]
```

```{.txt}
9
N
s
Nim
```

`s[^1]` points at the last element; `^n` is sugar for `s.len - n`. Because `s[0]` yields a `char`,
not a one-letter string, operators that work on `char` (such as `.ord`) apply directly. Reading an
index out of range does not return `nil`; Nim stops the program at runtime with an `IndexDefect`.

## Slicing

A slice of text is taken with a range inside square brackets. Both ends are included.

```{.nim}
let s = "Nim rocks"

echo s[0..2]     # "Nim"
echo s[4..8]     # "rocks"
echo s[^5..^1]   # "rocks", counted from the end
echo s[1..^2]    # "im rock"
```

```{.txt}
Nim
rocks
rocks
im rock
```

A range `a..b` means from index `a` through `b`, both included. Since `^n` counts from the back,
`s[^5..^1]` takes the last five characters. Slicing produces a new string; the original is
untouched.

## `&` versus `add`

There are two ways to join text, and the difference is about time and memory.

```{.nim}
var greeting = "Hello"
greeting.add(", ")
greeting.add("Nim")
echo greeting

let shout = greeting & "!"
echo shout
echo "count: " & $shout.len
```

```{.txt}
Hello, Nim
Hello, Nim!
count: 11
```

`add` appends straight to the string that already exists. Because that changes the value,
`greeting` must be a `var`. The `&` operator builds a new string from both sides without touching
the old one, so `shout` may be a `let`. When joining many pieces in a row, `add` is cheaper because
it does not copy everything again each time. A chain like `a & b & c` builds a temporary string at
every step, while `add` grows one buffer in place.

## Why `s[0] = 'N'` is rejected

A Nim string can be changed in place, but only when its binding is a `var`. Save this as
`mutation.nim`:

```{.nim}
let s = "nim"
s[0] = 'N'
echo s
```

```{.txt}
mutation.nim(2, 2) Error: 's[0]' cannot be assigned to
```

The message points at line 2, column 2, right at `[0]`. What is rejected is the assignment to an
element, not the string itself: `s` was made with `let`, so no part of it may change. Change `let`
to `var` and the program runs, printing `Nim`.

## Trimming and splitting text

Everyday tasks such as cleaning whitespace and splitting a CSV line live in `std/strutils`.

```{.nim}
import std/strutils

let csv = "alpha, beta, gamma"
let parts = csv.split(',')

echo parts.len
echo "[" & parts[1] & "]"
echo "[" & parts[1].strip & "]"
echo "[" & "  padded  ".strip & "]"
```

```{.txt}
3
[ beta]
[beta]
[padded]
```

`split` breaks a string into a `seq[string]` at each separator. Note the pieces still hold the
space after the comma; `strip` removes whitespace at both ends. The output lines are wrapped in
brackets so that the spaces do not silently disappear.

## Exercises

1. Print a single string that contains a double quote and a backslash, using the right escapes.
2. Without running it, predict the output:
   ```{.nim}
   echo "a" & "b" & "c"
   echo "abc".len
   ```
3. Write the path `C:\temp\new` using a raw string, then print it.
4. The code below fails. Fix it, then explain why it fails:
   ```{.nim}
   let s = "abc"
   s.add("d")
   echo s
   ```
5. Take the last three characters of `"programming"` with slicing, then print the result.

Answers are in [Appendix A](../appendix/answers.qmd).

## Summary

- `\n`, `\"`, and `\\` are escapes in an ordinary string; `r"..."` turns them off.
- Three quotes build a multi-line string, and the newline after the opener counts.
- `len` gives the number of bytes, indexing starts at zero, and `^n` counts from the back.
- `add` changes a string in place (needs `var`); `&` builds a new string.
- `split` and `strip` from `std/strutils` break and clean text.
